args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

MEMORANDUM

TO: Deal Team
FROM: Antitrust & Competition Practice
RE: Antitrust Risk Assessment and HSR Filing Strategy — Industrial Gas Distribution Acquisition
DATE: January 15, 2026

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

We have reviewed the deal materials for the proposed acquisition of an industrial gas distribution business by a private equity fund and assessed the antitrust risk profile arising from the horizontal overlap between the acquirer's portfolio and the target. This memorandum sets forth (i) our antitrust risk assessment under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976 ("HSR Act") and the substantive merger review framework, (ii) a reconciliation of the counterparty's markup against the base materials and the disclosure schedules, and (iii) a recommended HSR filing strategy.

Key takeaways:

• The transaction involves a horizontal overlap in the distribution of industrial gases, which will require careful market definition and competitive effects analysis.
• The matter is further complicated by two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed at Schedule 3.7 that intersect the Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") carve-outs proposed in the counterparty's markup.
• Schedule 5.2 identifies retained liabilities that the counterparty's indemnification changes would silently shift to the buyer.
• Exhibit B establishes a survival matrix for representations and warranties that the counterparty's limitation-period change directly contradicts.
• Per the controlling deal-team instruction (latest partner email superseding earlier directives), the client will concede the basket conversion (deductible to tipping basket) but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue.

II. TRANSACTION OVERVIEW

A. The Parties

The acquirer is a private equity fund (the "PE Fund") that holds portfolio investments in the industrial gas distribution sector. Through existing portfolio companies, the PE Fund (together with its controlled affiliates and portfolio companies, "Buyer") engages in the supply, distribution, and logistical handling of bulk and packaged industrial gases.

The target is an industrial gas distribution business ("Target") that operates in overlapping product and geographic markets with Buyer's existing portfolio companies. The Target provides bulk gas delivery, cylinder management, and on-site industrial gas supply services.

B. The Transaction

The transaction is structured as a stock purchase (or equivalent acquisition of equity interests) through which Buyer would acquire all of the equity of Target. The transaction requires HSR notification if the size-of-transaction and size-of-person thresholds under the HSR Act are satisfied. The current HSR thresholds (as adjusted annually for changes in the gross national product) will need to be verified as of the expected filing date. As structured, the transaction is expected to trigger the HSR premerger notification requirements.

C. Horizontal Overlap

The critical antitrust issue is the horizontal overlap between Buyer's existing industrial gas distribution operations and Target's business. The overlap spans both product dimensions (bulk gases, packaged gases, cylinder and container supply) and geographic dimensions (various regional distribution territories). This overlap gives rise to the principal substantive antitrust questions of this engagement: the definition of the relevant product and geographic markets, the measurement of market shares and concentration, the assessment of competitive effects, and the evaluation of entry conditions and efficiency justifications.

III. ANTITRUST RISK ASSESSMENT

A. Market Definition

The first analytical step is defining the relevant product market(s) and geographic market(s). For industrial gas distribution, the following considerations are relevant:

• Product markets: Industrial gases are typically segmented into bulk gases (delivered by tanker truck, including oxygen, nitrogen, argon, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen) and packaged gases (delivered in cylinders or other containers). These may constitute separate relevant product markets, or further sub-segments may be distinct (e.g., medical-grade gases vs. industrial-grade gases; on-site supply vs. delivered supply). Accordingly, the antitrust analysis must undertake a careful product-market definition analysis using the hypothetical monopolist test under the Horizontal Merger Guidelines.

• Geographic markets: Industrial gas distribution is commonly analyzed on a regional or local geographic basis due to transportation costs, the need for proximate distribution infrastructure, and the economics of tanker delivery. Relevant geographic markets may be defined at a regional level within the United States, with potential sub-regions or local metropolitan areas depending on the specific products and logistics.

B. Competitive Effects

Horizontal Merger Guidelines analysis should evaluate whether the transaction is likely to cause unilateral or coordinated effects that substantially lessen competition in the relevant markets.

• Unilateral effects: Where Buyer's portfolio companies and Target compete head-to-head in particular markets, the transaction may enable the combined entity to unilaterally raise prices or reduce service quality in markets where the combined market share is significant and where the parties are each other's closest competitors.

• Coordinated effects: In markets that are already concentrated or have favorable conditions for coordination (e.g., transparent pricing, homogeneous products, stable demand), the elimination of Target as a competitor could facilitate coordinated interaction among remaining firms.

The analysis requires a thorough review of company-level market share data, competitive overlap assessments, customer concentration data, bidding data and win/loss records, and testimony from customers and competitors.

C. Entry and Expansion

The competitive effects assessment must also consider whether potential entry or expansion by other firms would be timely, likely, and sufficient to deter or counteract any anticompetitive effects. In the industrial gas distribution industry, entry barriers may include the capital cost of distribution infrastructure (trucks, cylinders, filling plants), the need for established customer relationships and contracts, regulatory permits and safety requirements, and the economics of scale necessary for competitive delivery.

D. Pending Regulatory Inquiries — Schedule 3.7

Schedule 3.7 of the base materials discloses two pending regulatory inquiries affecting the Target. These inquiries are directly relevant to the antitrust risk assessment and to the transaction's risk profile for two distinct reasons.

First, the inquiries themselves may bear on the competitive landscape. If one or more of the inquiries relates to competition or market behavior in the industrial gas sector, the inquiries could signal existing competitive concerns in the markets where the parties overlap, potentially elevating the antitrust scrutiny applied to this transaction.

Second, Schedule 3.7's disclosure of these inquiries intersects with the counterparty's proposed MAE carve-outs. As discussed in Section IV below, the counterparty seeks to add carve-outs to the MAE definition for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter" — i.e., regulatory action that could flow from the two disclosed pending inquiries, or from the HSR/antitrust review itself. This is a critical drafting issue because the carve-outs would effectively eliminate Buyer's ability to invoke an MAE if a regulatory action arising from the disclosed inquiries causes a material adverse change in the Target's business. We analyze this in depth below.

E. Retained Liabilities — Schedule 5.2

Schedule 5.2 enumerates retained liabilities that the parties have agreed will remain with certain parties post-closing. These include, among other items, liabilities related to the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7, as well as other identified exposures. The scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials per the governing principles of the schedules and exhibits.

The retained liabilities in Schedule 5.2 must be carefully cross-referenced against the counterparty's proposed indemnification changes. As discussed below, the indemnification modifications in the markup would effectively shift portions of these retained liabilities to the buyer, contrary to the allocation reflected in the schedules. This is a material deviation from the agreed risk allocation that must be addressed in negotiations.

IV. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP — RECONCILIATION AND DEVIATION ANALYSIS

The counterparty's markup accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three material deviations from the base materials. Each must be analyzed and reconciled against the base documents, the disclosure schedules, and the controlling client instructions.

A. Deviation 1: Indemnification Cap Reduction and Basket Conversion

1. Description of the Markup Change

The counterparty's markup (i) silently reduces the indemnification cap, and (ii) converts the indemnity basket from a deductible to a tipping basket.

A deductible basket operates on an "all-or-nothing" basis: the indemnitor bears no liability until losses exceed the basket threshold, at which point the indemnitee may recover only the amount above the threshold (the threshold is never pierced). A tipping basket operates differently: once aggregate losses exceed the threshold, the indemnitee may recover all losses from the first dollar, including the amount below the basket threshold. The conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket is therefore more favorable to the indemnitee (the buyer in most acquisition structures) and unfavorable to the indemnitor (the seller).

2. Reconciliation Against Base Materials and Schedules

The base materials set the indemnification cap at a specific amount (the "Firm Standard Cap") and provided for a deductible basket. The counterparty's markup reduces the cap from the Firm Standard Cap to a lower amount (the "Markup Reduced Cap") while simultaneously converting the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket.

Schedule 5.2 is directly implicated. The retained liabilities listed in Schedule 5.2 include exposures that, under the base materials, were allocated to the seller and subject to the seller's indemnification obligations. The combination of (i) a reduced cap and (ii) a conversion to a tipping basket produces a net economic effect on the buyer that must be evaluated in the aggregate:

• The reduced cap decreases the buyer's maximum recovery from the seller.
• The tipping basket increases the buyer's recovery for losses below the original threshold.

These changes interact. For moderate loss amounts (between the basket threshold and the reduced cap), the tipping basket benefits the buyer. For larger loss amounts, the reduced cap disadvantages the buyer by capping recovery at a lower dollar figure. The net effect depends on the expected loss distribution and the magnitude of the pending regulatory inquiry liabilities.

Additionally, Schedule 5.2 enumerates retained liabilities including certain regulatory exposures. A reduced cap could leave the buyer under-compensated for these scheduled liabilities if those liabilities materialize into claims exceeding the reduced cap, particularly when cross-referenced with the two pending regulatory inquiries in Schedule 3.7.

3. Client Controlling Instruction

The controlling deal-team instruction (the latest partner email, which supersedes all earlier conflicting emails) states that the client will concede the basket conversion. This means the client accepts turning the deductible into a tipping basket. The client's concession on this point is firm and should not be re-litigated in negotiations.

However, the client's concession on the basket conversion does not extend to the cap reduction. The reduced indemnification cap remains an open issue for negotiation. The two elements (cap reduction and basket conversion) must be treated discretely: the client concedes the basket conversion; the client does not concede the cap reduction. The cap reduction, standing alone, materially impairs the buyer's indemnification protection and should be rejected or negotiated back to the Firm Standard Cap, particularly given the enumerated Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities.

4. Recommended Position

• Basket conversion (deductible to tipping): ACCEPT, per the controlling client instruction.
• Indemnification cap reduction: REJECT. Negotiate to restore the cap to the Firm Standard Cap. If concessions are necessary, consider a partial restoration or additional carve-outs tied to the Schedule 3.7 pending regulatory inquiries.

B. Deviation 2: Material Adverse Effect Definition — Regulatory Action Carve-Outs

1. Description of the Markup Change

The counterparty's markup adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter." In the context of an acquisition that requires HSR review and faces pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7, this language is dangerously broad.

2. Reconciliation Against Base Materials and Schedules

The base MAE definition follows the firm-standard formulation, which is comprehensive but does not include carve-outs for the type of regulatory action contemplated by the markup. The proposed carve-outs would operate to exclude from the MAE definition any material adverse effect caused by:

• Regulatory action stemming from or relating to the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7;
• Regulatory action arising from the HSR review process itself, including second request investigations or the imposition of conditions;
• Any other regulatory action "of the kind at issue" in this matter.

The effect of these carve-outs is twofold:

First, they would deprive Buyer of MAE termination rights if the pending regulatory inquiries escalate and materially harm Target's business between signing and closing. If the two pending inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7 result in fines, penalties, injunctions, or business restrictions that materially impair the Target's operations, Buyer would be unable to terminate the transaction on MAE grounds under the markup's proposed carve-outs.

Second, because Schedule 3.7 discloses the two pending inquiries, the carve-outs are not abstract or hypothetical — they are specifically tailored to remove the very real risks that were identified and disclosed during due diligence. This is precisely the kind of risk allocation that should remain with the seller through the indemnification provisions and the MAE definition.

The scheduled exceptions in the disclosure schedules (which control over general statements) confirm that the two pending regulatory inquiries are known and identified risks. The carve-outs would effectively assign the downside of those known risks to the buyer without corresponding compensation.

3. Recommended Position

REJECT the MAE carve-outs in their current form. The carve-outs would eliminate buyer protection for the specifically disclosed regulatory risks that the parties have already identified. If the seller insists on some form of regulatory carve-out, we recommend:

• Limiting any carve-out to regulatory action arising solely from HSR approval conditions negotiated by the parties (not from third-party initiated regulatory action);
• Excluding from any carve-out regulatory action arising from or relating to the two pending inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7;
• Requiring specific disclosure of any regulatory action intended to be covered by a carve-out, rather than generic "of the kind at issue" language.

C. Deviation 3: Shortened Survival Period for Core Representations

1. Description of the Markup Change

The counterparty's markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival of the core representations (including representations relating to the pending regulatory inquiries, financial statements, and compliance matters), contradicting the survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B.

2. Reconciliation Against Exhibit B

Exhibit B establishes the survival matrix for representations and warranties. Under the base materials, core representations — including those relating to regulatory compliance, financial statements, and the accuracy of the disclosure schedules — survive for the full statutory or agreed limitation period, with a subset of "fundamental" representations surviving indefinitely or for the full statute of limitations. The shorter survival matrix in the counterparty's markup directly contradicts Exhibit B's schedule.

The conflict is significant because the scheduled exceptions in the disclosure schedules control over general statements in the base materials. Exhibit B represents the agreed risk allocation between the parties regarding the time period within which the indemnitee may bring claims for breach. Shortening the survival period for core representations would:

• Reduce the buyer's ability to bring indemnification claims for breaches that are not discovered within the shortened period;
• Particularly problematic given the Schedule 3.7 pending regulatory inquiries, as regulatory compliance issues may take time to surface, investigate, and quantify;
• Inconsistent with the buyer's indemnification exposure to the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities.

3. Client Controlling Instruction

The controlling deal-team instruction is explicit and firm: the client treats any survival-period reduction as a WALK-AWAY issue. This is the highest-priority red line in the negotiation. The client will not close on terms that shorten the survival period for core representations.

4. Recommended Position

REJECT the survival-period reduction. This is a walk-away issue per the client's controlling instruction. We recommend:

• Maintaining the survival matrix as set forth in Exhibit B;
• Treating any shortening of the survival period for core representations (including representations regarding regulatory matters disclosed in Schedule 3.7) as non-negotiable;
• Communicating clearly to the counterparty that this provision is a deal-breaker, not merely a bargainable point.

D. Summary of Deviations and Recommended Positions

| Deviation | Counterparty Change | Recommended Position | Basis |
|-----------|-------------------|---------------------|-------|
| 1a. Indemnification cap | Reduced from Firm Standard | REJECT — restore to Firm Standard Cap | Schedule 5.2 allocations; client instruction concedes only basket conversion |
| 1b. Basket | Deductible → tipping | ACCEPT | Client controlling instruction |
| 2. MAE carve-outs | Added regulatory action carve-outs | REJECT — narrow or eliminate | Schedule 3.7 disclosures; carve-outs tailored to existing known risks |
| 3. Survival period | Shortened for core reps | REJECT — WALK-AWAY issue | Client controlling instruction; contradicts Exhibit B |

V. HSR FILING STRATEGY

A. HSR Act Applicability

The proposed acquisition of Target by Buyer will be subject to the premerger notification and waiting period requirements of the HSR Act if the transaction value and party size exceed the applicable thresholds. The PE Fund structure requires specific attention to the determination of the ultimate parent entity and the aggregation of holdings across controlled portfolio companies.

B. Key Threshold Considerations

• Size-of-Transaction Test: The acquisition price for Target must exceed the current size-of-transaction threshold. Based on the deal structure (full acquisition of equity), this test is expected to be satisfied.

• Size-of-Person Test: Unless an exception applies (e.g., a person's total assets or annual net sales are below the applicable floor), the size-of-person test must also be satisfied. The PE Fund and its portfolio companies are expected to meet this test.

• Because both the size-of-transaction and size-of-person tests are met, an HSR filing is required before closing. The parties must observe the 30-calendar-day waiting period (which may be extended by a request for additional information or documentary material, commonly known as a "second request").

C. Filing Responsibilities and Structure

The ultimate parent entity of the acquiring person must be determined for HSR purposes. For a PE fund structure, the general partner or fund manager and each controlled portfolio company within the "acquiring person" must be analyzed. The acquiring persons must be properly defined and all required information (including revenues by NAICS code, prior acquisitions, and documents regarding market analysis) must be compiled.

D. Timing and Strategy

Given the horizontal overlap and the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7, we recommend a proactive filing strategy:

1. Early Preparation: Begin assembling the substantive HSR documentation immediately, including competitive overlap analyses, market share data, and any analyses of market dynamics prepared for the deal. These materials may become subject to second-request scrutiny.

2. Early Filing: File the HSR notification early in the diligence process to maximize the available waiting period and to allow time for the agencies to review and, if necessary, issue a second request.

3. Proactive Engagement: Consider early engagement with the antitrust agencies (FTC or DOJ) through a pre-merger process or informal communications to gauge their level of concern about the horizontal overlap and to potentially shorten the overall review timeline.

4. Second Request Preparedness: Given the horizontal overlap and the pending regulatory inquiries, a second request is a realistic possibility. We recommend preparing a second-request response infrastructure early, including document collection processes and data management for potential competitive effects analyses.

5. Remedial Planning: If the agencies express concerns regarding specific markets, we should be prepared to discuss remedies, including divestiture of overlapping assets, behavioral commitments, or other conditions. The antitrust risk assessment should inform the price-structure walk-away analysis, particularly given the client's position on the survival-period walk-away issue.

E. Interplay with Agreed Risk Allocation

The HSR review and the companion regulatory inquiries create timing and outcome uncertainty. The indemnification provisions and the MAE definition are directly consequential: if the antitrust review extends, if a second request is issued, or if the pending regulatory inquiries escalate, the contractual risk allocation determines which party bears the consequences.

The counterparty's markup attempts to exploit these uncertainties by (i) carving out regulatory action from the MAE definition, (ii) reducing the indemnification cap to limit exposure even if regulatory liabilities materialize, and (iii) shortening survival to limit the window for claims. All three deviate from the base materials' risk allocation. The client's positions on each as set forth above are squarely aligned with preserving the intended allocation.

VI. RECOMMENDED NEXT STEPS

1. Immediately communicate the counterparty markup analysis to the deal team, with particular emphasis on the walk-away nature of the survival-period reduction per the client's controlling instruction.

2. Prepare a formal response/redline to the counterparty that:
   • Accepts the basket conversion (deductible to tipping basket), consistent with the client's concession;
   • Rejects the indemnification cap reduction and restores the Firm Standard Cap;
   • Rejects the MAE carve-outs or, at minimum, narrows them to exclude the Schedule 3.7-disclosed regulatory inquiries;
   • Rejects any survival-period reduction and maintains Exhibit B's survival matrix.

3. Commence HSR filing preparation, including assembling competitive analyses, market share data, and organizational charts.

4. Coordinate with outside counsel and diligence teams on the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7 to assess potential impact on timing and risk allocation.

5. Develop a second-request contingency plan, including document collection protocols and data management infrastructure, given the realistic prospect of extended merger review.

VII. CONCLUSION

This acquisition presents a meaningful antitrust risk profile due to the horizontal overlap in industrial gas distribution, coupled with the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7. The counterparty's markup introduces three material deviations that would erode the buyer's negotiated protections precisely where those protections matter most. The client's controlling instructions require concession on the basket conversion but treat survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue; the cap reduction and MAE carve-outs are each separately adverse and should be rejected. The HSR filing strategy should be proactive, with early filing and second-request preparedness as central elements.

***

This memorandum reflects a preliminary antitrust risk assessment based on the materials provided. Additional analysis will be required as market data, share information, and further details regarding the pending regulatory inquiries become available. This memorandum is privileged and confidential and is provided solely for the use of the client in connection with the evaluation of the proposed transaction.
